design.title: Reading a limestone cave

goal.text: Students use field evidence to explain how a limestone cave and its formations are made, and what that evidence says about the past

learnerProfile.text: Year 9 earth science students (age 13-14) at the end of a unit on rocks and weathering. Mixed reading levels
learnerProfile.priorKnowledge: The rock cycle, and that acids react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide

learnerRole.text: Explain to a new volunteer cave guide what the evidence in the cave shows, so the guide can explain it to visitors accurately

character.name: Dana Okafor
character.role: a new volunteer guide who starts leading school tours next week and is worried about saying something wrong

materials.name: Unit handout: karst and caves
materials.text: Limestone is made mostly of the mineral calcite, which is calcium carbonate. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil and becomes a weak carbonic acid. This slightly acidic water seeps into cracks and slowly dissolves limestone; over hundreds of thousands of years the cracks widen into caves. A drop of dilute hydrochloric acid on limestone fizzes because the calcite reacts and releases carbon dioxide gas; a rock that does not fizz is not limestone. When water carrying dissolved calcite drips into the cave air it loses carbon dioxide and can no longer hold all of its calcite, so a thin film of calcite is deposited. Stalactites grow down from the ceiling and stalagmites grow up from the floor where the drips land. Stalagmites grow very slowly, typically about 0.1 millimetres per year, so a stalagmite two metres tall is roughly twenty thousand years old. Limestone forms on shallow sea floors from lime mud and the skeletons of sea animals; fossils such as crinoid stems and shells in a cave wall show the rock was once a sea floor. A landscape shaped by dissolving rock is called karst.

stakes.text: the guide will repeat whatever they are told to hundreds of visitors, including any mistakes

criteria.text: Explains that slightly acidic water dissolves limestone and uses the acid fizz test as evidence the rock is calcite

activation: Before you begin: in your own words, what do you already know about "Reading a limestone cave"?
Which idea from earlier lessons do you expect to need most here, and why?

practice.opening: Hi, I'm Dana. I'm a new volunteer guide who starts leading school tours next week and is worried about saying something wrong. I was told you can help me understand this. I really am starting from zero, so go slowly.

challenges.prompt: Here's something I don't understand yet: slightly, acidic and water. How would you explain it to me?
challenges.harder: Okay, I think I follow. But suppose someone disagreed with you. What would you say to convince them?
support: I'm lost. Could you try again with one concrete example?
Go back to the course material you read before we started. Which part deals with slightly, acidic and water? What does it imply here?

challenges.harder: Okay, I think I follow. But suppose someone disagreed with you. What would you say to convince them?

Go back to the course material you read before we started. Which part deals with fossils, wall and evidence? What does it imply here?

probes.voice: Oh! So does that mean caves are carved by fast flowing rivers cutting through the rock?
probes.challenge: Hold on. A moment ago you said something that sounded like "caves are carved by fast flowing rivers cutting through the rock". If that were true, what would we expect to see? Does that match what you know?

probes.voice: Oh! So does that mean stalactites and stalagmites are made of ice or frozen water?
probes.challenge: Hold on. A moment ago you said something that sounded like "stalactites and stalagmites are made of ice or frozen water". If that were true, what would we expect to see? Does that match what you know?

practice.closing: Thank you. I think I could explain some of this to someone else now.
practice.refusal: I can't tell you the answer; I'm the one who doesn't know it! Try explaining the part you're surest of.

selfAssessment: Before you see any feedback: how do you think that went? Which moment are you most satisfied with?
What would you do differently if you did it again?
feedback.transfer: A different situation: a sea cliff with layered rock and fossils that you visit on holiday. What from this session would you use there, and what would you change?

prompts.character:
You play Dana Okafor, a new volunteer guide who starts leading school tours next week and is worried about saying something wrong, in a teachback for these learners: Year 9 earth science students (age 13-14) at the end of a unit on rocks and weathering. Mixed reading levels.
Learning goal (do not drift from it): Students use field evidence to explain how a limestone cave and its formations are made, and what that evidence says about the past
The learner's job: Explain to a new volunteer cave guide what the evidence in the cave shows, so the guide can explain it to visitors accurately
Stakes: the guide will repeat whatever they are told to hundreds of visitors, including any mistakes
Difficulty: gentle. Help policy: questions-then-materials.
Stay in character. Never give the answer or do the learner's work. Raise the challenge only after the learner shows evidence; give support only as the help policy allows.
Classroom constraints (for you, never say them aloud): Do not use the word 'erosion' when you mean dissolving
Teacher notes: none
prompts.assessor:
Record evidence only for these educator-approved criteria, quoting the learner's own words:
- c1: Explains that slightly acidic water dissolves limestone and uses the acid fizz test as evidence the rock is calcite (look for: slightly, acidic, water, dissolves, limestone, uses, acid, fizz, test, evidence, rock, calcite)
- c2: Explains that stalactites and stalagmites grow when dripping water loses carbon dioxide and deposits calcite (look for: stalactites, stalagmites, grow, dripping, water, loses, carbon, dioxide, deposits, calcite, limestone, acid)
- c3: Uses a measurement and a growth rate to estimate how old a formation is (look for: measurement, growth, rate, estimate, formation)
- c4: Uses fossils in the wall as evidence that the limestone formed on an ancient sea floor (look for: fossils, wall, evidence, limestone, formed, ancient, floor, grow, carbonate, stalactites, stalagmites, skeletons)
Watch for these misconceptions:
- m1: Caves are carved by fast flowing rivers cutting through the rock
- m2: Stalactites and stalagmites are made of ice or frozen water
Do not assess anything the learner was not asked to do. Mark observation separately from inference.
prompts.feedback: Write feedback for the learning goal "Students use field evidence to explain how a limestone cave and its formations are made, and what that evidence says about the past". Ask for self-assessment first. For each criterion cite the learner's actual words and the turn they came from. Say "not assessed" where the learner had no fair opportunity. Offer concrete next actions and finish with the transfer question.
